thread.text: The question is the modeled probability a claimed significant relationship is true. “Finding” here means a relationship reaching formal statistical significance.
The base framework combines prior true-to-null odds R, power 1−β and Type I error α into PPV, then extends to bias u and testing by multiple teams.
Corollaries are conditional; Table 4 contains model scenarios, and the null-field argument is a thought experiment, not a diagnosis of every real field.
Proposals include stronger evidence and less bias; large studies may retain bias, and assumptions about R may be subjective.

sections.title: Framework: from true-positive counts to PPV
sections.role: Defines tested relationships and power, then asks what fraction of claimed findings are true.

points.text: R is the ratio of true to null relationships, not itself a probability; prior probability is R/(1+R). For simplicity the author considers one true relationship or similar power across true relationships.

sections.learning_goal: Derive PPV from Table 1 and distinguish prior odds, power and probability of truth after significance

visuals.title: Table 1 and the base PPV formula

purpose.text: Explain why α=.05 does not mean a finding has a 95% probability of truth.

reading.text: Verified Table 1 on PDF page2: rows indicate claimed finding, columns truth. PPV is computed along the finding=Yes row.

contribution.text: In the unbiased single-testing framework, PPV exceeds one half when (1−β)R>α; this is not an observed frequency for all fields.

steps.text: The numerator weights true positives; the denominator adds false positives. Common factor c/(R+1) cancels.
With low R, false positives can occupy a large share of significant findings even with substantial power.

sections.title: Bias: turning non-findings into claims
sections.role: Extends the counting framework and separates bias from chance.

points.text: u is the proportion of analyses that would not be findings but are presented as such through bias; the model assumes u does not depend on truth, not that u was measured for each real study.

sections.title: Multiple teams: selecting at least one significant result
sections.role: Changes the event being selected; this is distinct from combining all evidence.

points.text: The model concerns at least one significant result among n independent equal-power tests; it does not claim that consistent independent confirmation lowers credibility.

sections.title: Six corollaries and their interactions
sections.role: Links power, prior odds and bias changes to research practices.

points.text: The author discusses small studies, small effects, broad unselected testing, flexible analyses, interests and hot fields. Factors interact: a hot field can also promote larger studies and improved standards.

sections.title: Model scenarios and null-field thought experiment
sections.role: Distinguishes parameter-based predictions from empirical surveys.

points.text: Table 4 computes PPV from stipulated power, R and u. The null-field passage assumes no true relationships before discussing deviations; it cannot directly establish that a real field is entirely false.

sections.title: Improvement and references: contextualize isolated findings
sections.role: Turns critique into conditional proposals; cited works were not independently read.

points.text: Better-powered, low-bias evidence may help, but large studies can retain bias. The totality of evidence matters more than one team’s significant result; estimating prior odds still involves subjective assumptions.

explanation.text: Here, probability a relationship is true conditional on a claimed finding; neither power nor 1−p.
True relationships divided by null relationships; prior probability is R/(1+R).
Probability of detection when a relationship is true; reverses the conditioning direction compared with PPV.
Proportion of otherwise non-findings presented as findings; a model parameter, not a universal bias measurement.
Thought experiment assuming no true relationships; cannot simply be imposed on an actual field.
